extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, students of literature, poets, and educated readers interested in criticism and the study of poetry
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for critics on the right tone, purpose, methods, and standards in literary criticism and in the study and judgment of poetry. Emphasises disinterestedness, high aesthetic standards, breadth of knowledge, and specific cautions about common mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticism defined as disinterested endeavour
rubrics_metrics.description: "a disinterested endeavor to learn and propagate the best that is known and thought in the world."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is presented as the critic's proper function: to seek and spread the best ideas and knowledge without practical or partisan aims. The essay contrasts this ideal with critics who act as partisans or who alter critic's aims to suit practical movements (e.g., 'the liberal party'). The critic's work is intellectual and moral, not primarily political or social activism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain independence from the practical spirit
rubrics_metrics.description: "Criticism must maintain its independence of the practical spirit and its aims."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not subordinate their judgments to immediate practical utility, party interests, or social movements. The text warns against critics joining 'the party movement' or applauding everything in a movement; instead critics should be perpetually dissatisfied when works fall short of ideal, even if practically useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt detachment and indirect, patient action
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism should embrace 'the Indian virtue of detachment' and 'abandoning the sphere of practical life', accepting a 'slow and obscure' influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author advises a subtle, indirect approach: by remaining collected and disinterested, the critic slowly alters perspectives rather than engaging in immediate practical combat. This patient, indirect action is the only proper work of criticism, even if it is slow to change mass opinion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use stark contrast to expose excessive claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism may use juxtaposition (contrast) to moderate grandiose or self-congratulatory claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: juxtaposing boastful national eulogies (Sir Charles Adderley, Mr. Roebuck) with a brief news item—'A shocking child murder ... Wragg is in custody'—to show the limitations and harshness contained within triumphant claims. Such contrasts can force moderation in extravagant assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise knowledge — fresh, wide, and especially foreign
rubrics_metrics.description: "knowledge, and ever fresh knowledge, must be the critic's great concern for himself." and "the English critic of literature, therefore, must dwell much on foreign thought"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should constantly acquire new knowledge and have a broad acquaintance with other literatures (Greek, Roman, Eastern, and at least one great literature besides their own). Fresh learning should lead the critic's work; judgment should follow as a secondary, accompanying activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let knowledge lead; keep judgment subsidiary
rubrics_metrics.description: Communicate fresh knowledge and let one's 'own judgment pass along with it,--but insensibly, and in the second place, not the first.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preferred method of influencing readers is to present knowledge first; allow the critic's judgment to follow unobtrusively rather than proclaiming abstract rules. This makes criticism more persuasive and productive of genuine understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set and keep a high standard for poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Because poetry's destiny is high, 'we must also set our standard for poetry high, since poetry... must be poetry of a high order of excellence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given poetry's role as 'the breath and finer spirit of all knowledge' and its future importance in interpreting life, critics should judge poetry by strict, elevated standards. Expect strictness and demand excellence from poets; the best poetry is what is truly wanted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the inviolability of poetry; exclude charlatanism
rubrics_metrics.description: "In poetry... it is the glory, the eternal honor, that charlatanism shall find no entrance; that this noble sphere be kept inviolate and inviolable."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid any confusion or obliteration of the distinction between excellent and inferior, true and untrue. Charlatanism—whether conscious or unconscious—obscures these distinctions and must be guarded against in poetry criticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the historic-estimate fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware the fallacy where a poet or poem is over-rated 'because [it] counts to us historically' as a stage in development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studying a poet's historical role can incline a critic to praise works more highly than their intrinsic poetic quality warrants. Maintain separation between historical interest and pure poetic value to prevent exaggerated praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid the personal-estimate fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware the fallacy where a poet or poem is over-rated 'on grounds personal to ourselves' because of private affinities or circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal taste, emotional connections, or private importance can lead critics to overrate a poet. Critics must watch for personal bias and strive for impartiality in assessing intrinsic merit.

rubrics_metrics.name: When required, be chiefly judgmental but avoid abstraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes criticism 'may have to deal with a subject-matter so familiar that fresh knowledge is out of the question, and then it must be all judgment; an enunciation and detailed application of principles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In such cases the critic's work is to state principles and apply them, but the 'great safeguard is never to let oneself become abstract'—retain a lively consciousness of the truth of what one says to avoid tautology and sterile analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be patient, flexible, and know when to attach or withdraw
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism 'must be patient, and know how to wait; and flexible, and know how to attach itself to things and how to withdraw from them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not rush ideas into practice; they should mature ideas and be ready to advance them when appropriate. Flexibility includes praising elements useful for 'spiritual perfection' even if those elements belong to powers that are practically harmful, and likewise exposing spiritual shortcomings in practically beneficent powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discern spiritual qualities apart from practical benefit
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism 'must be apt to study and praise elements that for the fulness of spiritual perfection are wanted, even though they belong to a power which in the practical sphere may be maleficent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should be able to praise aspects that contribute to spiritual or ideal excellence even when those aspects come from movements or institutions that are practically problematic, and to criticize practically useful institutions for spiritual defects (examples: English Divorce Court vs. Catholic marriage theory).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivate personal virtues: sincerity, simplicity, ardor, expanding knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism 'must be sincere, simple, flexible, ardent, ever widening its knowledge.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These personal qualities are prerequisites for criticism to have a 'joyful sense of creative activity' and to be effective. Sincerity also helps to convince practical men of the critic's intentions and reduce misunderstandings born of perceived partisanship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritise the idea in poetry; attach emotion to idea
rubrics_metrics.description: "For poetry... the idea is everything; the rest is a world of illusion... Poetry attaches its emotion to the idea; the idea _is_ the fact."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying or judging poetry, the critic should value the conception or idea expressed by the poem above mere factual or superficial elements. The emotional investment of poetry should be tied to the idea; poetry's power lies in making idea the felt fact.
